title: From Gidófalva to the Pampa: the Youngest Honvéd General and the Surveyor of Argentina
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Gidófalva, the birth in Háromszék
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the eighth of June 1822 a son is born at Gidófalva, a Székely village in Háromszék, to a Habsburg cavalry officer who has broken his family's tradition by taking a commission. The Hungarian National Library will catalogue the boy as of Armenian origin, and the Armenian embassy in Buenos Aires will give his name as Hovhannes Tzetzian. Family tradition traces the line to settlers named Vartan who reached Transylvania about 1672, the name entered as Czetz at Szamosujvar in 1715. No register confirming any of it has surfaced. The attribution travels with him; the archive behind it stays empty.
suggested_refs: The Armenian merchant colonies of Szamosújvár and Gyergyószentmiklós, rooted in Transylvania since the seventeenth century
sources: Országos Széchényi Könyvtár catalogue attribution 'örmény származású', cited through the research brief and not fetched directly

stops.name: Kézdivásárhely, the institute at seven years old
stops.date_confidence: traditional; year approximate, given as 'around age seven'
stops.campa: The father dies early and the boy is sent, at about seven, into the military preparatory institute at Kézdivásárhely, a Székely market town in the east of Transylvania. He is set to Latin, German, geography and surveying, the last of which will feed him for forty years on another continent. It is the first gate of a system that will carry him through cadet schools to Wiener Neustadt and Vienna before he ever wears the honvéd colors he becomes known for. He enters it a Székely child of seven and comes out of the system thirteen years later, a lieutenant of imperial infantry.
suggested_refs: The Habsburg military preparatory institute at Kézdivásárhely (Târgu Secuiesc)

stops.name: Wiener Neustadt, first in his class
stops.date_confidence: attested for graduation and commission; the years of attendance are not itemized in the sources
stops.campa: Czetz completes the Theresian Military Academy at Wiener Neustadt, the empire's premier officer school, first in his class. The castle that houses it has turned out imperial officers for sixty years, and it turns him out in 1842 as a lieutenant, hadnagy, into the 62nd Infantry Regiment. He is a Hungarian fluent in the empire's language of command, top of a class trained to hold the empire together. Six years later he will be in the field against it, and the schooling he takes out of Wiener Neustadt is the schooling of the officers sent to stop him.
suggested_refs: The Theresianische Militärakademie in the castle of Wiener Neustadt

stops.name: Pest, the Magyar hadnyelvtan
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Two years after his commission, Trattner and Károlyi print at Pest a manual by the young lieutenant: Magyar hadnyelvtan, a Hungarian military language for officers of the imperial and royal army, arguing that troops should be commanded in the tongue they were born to. He is twenty-two. That same year his name is weighed for the Hungarian Academy of Sciences alongside János Korponay and Lázár Mészáros, and set down again without election, with encouraging words and nothing else. The book is an officer's technical work. It is also a position, printed and bound, four years before the position becomes a war.
stops.quote: Nothing so effectively emboldens an army as the personal presence of its commander, if he knows how to address it in its mother tongue.
stops.quote_source: János Czetz, Magyar Hadnyelvtan a császári és királyi osztriai hadsereg tisztjei számára (1844), quoted on hu.wikipedia, 'Czetz János'
suggested_refs: Magyar hadnyelvtan, Pest, Trattner-Károlyi Ny., 1844

stops.name: Vienna, the drafting table at the Cartographic Institute
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: In 1846 Czetz leaves the infantry line for the Geographical-Cartographic Institute in Vienna, the empire's mapping bureaucracy, and bends over a drafting table. It is a desk posting two years before the capital erupts. The surveying eye he sharpens here will resurface on the pampas fourteen years later, drawing the borders of Argentina with Paraguay and Brazil and staking a line of forts across grass no European has measured. In 1846 he is neither general nor exile, only a draughtsman on the imperial payroll with two years left of that.
suggested_refs: The Imperial Geographical-Cartographic Institute, Vienna

stops.name: Pest, out of the imperial corps
stops.date_confidence: month attested; the enlistment site is not documented and Pest is given as the seat of the honvéd ministry
stops.campa: In July 1848 Czetz leaves his Vienna post for the honvéd army the reform government is raising, and enters it as a senior captain, főszázados. The force he joins does not fully exist yet; the loyalty he changes is not a border he crosses but an oath he replaces. The sources give the month and no place, so Pest stands here as the ministry's seat and the likely point of transfer rather than a documented address. Karl Gräser, another Transylvanian who will leave a Habsburg commission and reinvent himself abroad, walks out of the same army half a century later toward Monte Verità and Ida Hofmann.
suggested_refs: The Hungarian War Ministry at Pest, summer 1848
sources: working/journeys/ida_hoffmann.journey.json (Karl Gräser, former Habsburg officer from Transylvania)

stops.name: The Bácska, the southern campaigns
stops.date_confidence: month attested; no town is named in any reachable source and the pin is the theatre, not a battlefield
stops.campa: Czetz is appointed to the War Ministry and serves that September in the southern campaigns under War Minister Lázár Mészáros, in the borderland between the Danube and the Tisza where Serb insurgent forces are contesting the southern counties. No source consulted names a single town he fought in. It is six weeks of undercharted service, and then he is pulled north and east into Transylvania, where the record turns precise and stays precise for the rest of the war.
suggested_refs: Lázár Mészáros's autumn 1848 operations in the Bácska

stops.name: Kolozsvár, temporary command of Transylvania
stops.date_confidence: date attested; the headquarters is inferred and probably wrong, since Kolozsvár fell to Wardener in mid-November
stops.campa: On the thirtieth of October 1848 Czetz is promoted major and given temporary command of the ten thousand Hungarian troops left in Transylvania. He is twenty-six and holds a province for a month. Kolozsvár is the region's military seat and the obvious guess at his headquarters, and the guess is probably wrong: the town falls to the Habsburg general Wardener in mid-November and the force retreats west. What he actually commands is an army in motion, reorganized and reinforced on the road, in the last weeks before a Pole arrives to take it from him and make it famous.
suggested_refs: Wardener's occupation of Kolozsvár, mid-November 1848

stops.name: The Csucsa pass, Puchner halted
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the action is attested to Czetz's November command but no source consulted gives an exact day
stops.campa: Pushed out of the interior, Czetz sets his line at the Csucsa pass, the mountain gate between the Great Hungarian Plain and Transylvania, and holds it against Puchner's advance. This is his own work, done before Bem arrives, and it is the reason there is still an army in the field to hand over. Later accounts will fold the action into Bem's campaign and credit the general with a pass his chief of staff had already closed. The line at Csucsa is what December is launched from, and the man standing on it in November is Czetz.
suggested_refs: The Csucsa (Ciucea) defile, gate between the Alföld and Transylvania

stops.name: Szilágysomlyó, the Pole addresses his officers
stops.date_confidence: attested for Bem's assumption of command on 1 December 1848; Czetz's appointment as chief of staff is dated 29 November
stops.campa: József Bem, sixty-four years old, veteran of Napoleon's Russia and of the Warsaw insurrection, takes command of the Transylvanian forces on the first of December and reviews his officer corps at Szilágysomlyó. He speaks, his new chief of staff records, in German with a Polish accent, and says three sentences that set the terms of the command. Czetz is twenty-six and writes them down. Twenty years later he prints them verbatim in Pest, in a book about the man he served, in Hungarian of his own making because Bem had none.
stops.quote: Gentlemen, I demand unconditional obedience from you; whoever disobeys, I will have shot. I know how to reward, but I also know how to punish. You may go!
stops.quote_source: József Bem, quoted by János Czetz in Bem erdélyi hadjárata 1848-49-ben (Pest, 1868), printed p. V; own translation from Hungarian
suggested_refs: Czetz, Bem erdélyi hadjárata 1848-49-ben (Pest, 1868), digitized at mek.oszk.hu/09600/09664
sources: Czetz, Bem erdélyi hadjárata 1848-49-ben (1868), p. V, verified verbatim in the digitized PDF

stops.name: The Csucsa pass, the winter offensive opens
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the eighteenth of December Bem takes the army standing at Csucsa, the army Czetz held there in November, and throws it east through the pass. Within weeks the counteroffensive clears most of Transylvania of imperial forces. Czetz rides beside the old general as chief of staff and drafts the operational plans; the speed is what the later accounts remember, and the plans behind the speed are his. He will publish the campaign's history from exile in Hamburg within two years of its end, and his own name will go into print attached to Bem's.
stops.quote: The Hungarians are brave, good, courageous men, resolute soldiers, but writing is not their affair. They would rather ride fifteen miles than write a single word.
stops.quote_source: József Bem, quoted by János Czetz in Bem erdélyi hadjárata 1848-49-ben (Pest, 1868), p. X; own translation from Hungarian
suggested_refs: Bem's winter campaign of 1848-1849 in Transylvania
sources: Czetz, Bem erdélyi hadjárata 1848-49-ben (1868), p. X

stops.name: The Marosvásárhely road, two hussars condemned
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the passage is undated in Czetz's book, and Marosvásárhely comes under Bem's control in January 1849
stops.campa: Two hussar non-commissioned officers disobey on the road to Marosvásárhely and are condemned to be shot. Two of their comrades step forward to plead for them, as custom allows, and Bem answers with two words. Then two officers of the same company plead, and he answers the same way. Only when Kiss Sándor, whom Czetz calls the bravest of the brave, intercedes does the old man lift the sentence. Czetz sets the scene down in a character sketch without a date, which is how the discipline of that army survives: not as an order, as an anecdote.
stops.quote_source: József Bem, quoted by János Czetz in Bem erdélyi hadjárata 1848-49-ben (Pest, 1868), p. VIII; own translation from Hungarian
suggested_refs: Czetz's character sketch of Bem, Bem erdélyi hadjárata, prefatory pages
sources: Czetz, Bem erdélyi hadjárata 1848-49-ben (1868), p. VIII, verified verbatim

stops.name: Medgyes, the first day held
stops.date_confidence: attested for the day; the engagement runs 2 to 3 March and the outcome of the second day reverses the first
stops.campa: Czetz has been a colonel for eighteen days when Puchner pushes toward the Saxon market town of Medgyes on the second of March, and he throws the advance back. That is the whole of what the record supports. The next day Bem, who is present, fights a bayonet action and evacuates the town. Hungarian accounts that hand Czetz a victorious battle in Bem's absence are describing something that did not happen. A holding action on the first day of a two-day engagement broken off on the second: that is the shape of it, and it still opens the road to Nagyszeben.
suggested_refs: hu.wikipedia, 'Medgyesi csata', on the two-day engagement of 2 to 3 March 1849

stops.name: Nagyszeben, the citadel taken
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the eleventh of March Nagyszeben falls, the Saxon citadel city that has anchored Habsburg power in southern Transylvania for centuries, with Czetz at the center of the operation as chief of staff. Bem recommends him for general on the strength of it. On the eighth of April comes the Hungarian Military Order of Merit, third class; in May the promotion is approved and he is the youngest general in the honvéd army, twenty-six years old. His commander's assessment of him survives in one sentence, though the sentence travels with a warning attached to its source.
stops.quote: Relentless severity, impartiality, harshness in punishment, but magnanimity in reward; free from vengefulness, from even the slightest shadow of selfishness.
stops.quote_source: József Bem on Czetz, as quoted on hu.wikipedia, 'Czetz János', after Jakab Erzsébet, rmcssz.ro; the words are absent from Czetz's Emlékezéseim, to which they are sometimes misattributed
suggested_refs: The Hungarian Military Order of Merit, third class, awarded 8 April 1849

stops.name: Kolozsvár, the fall from the horse
stops.date_confidence: date attested; the place of the accident is nowhere documented and Kolozsvár is the presumed seat of the acting command
stops.campa: On the twenty-ninth of May, acting as Transylvanian commander while Bem campaigns in the Banat, Czetz falls from his horse. The injury ends his combat role in the revolution three weeks after his general's rank is confirmed. No source consulted names the road, the town or the circumstances; a war career that the archive tracks day by day for six months stops on a date with no place attached to it. Everything after this he watches from the outside, first from hiding inside Hungary, then from Hamburg with a manuscript.
suggested_refs: Bem's Banat campaign of May 1849, during which Czetz held the Transylvanian command

stops.name: Déva, the officers bring their banner
stops.date_confidence: attested to August 1849; Czetz is not present, having been out of command since 29 May, and records the scene in his 1868 book
stops.campa: In the last hours before the Transylvanian army collapses, ten officers of the 37th battalion come to Bem at Déva with their banner in their hands and one sentence prepared. Czetz is not there. He is in hiding somewhere in Hungary with the Habsburg authorities looking for him. He writes the scene down nineteen years later from what he was told, and adds that the old general embraced them in tears. The banner is what they saved, and what they offer is to carry it as a funeral rite.
stops.quote: Vécsey has laid down his arms, our men have scattered, we have saved this sacred pledge of honor, and we are ready, General, to carry it under your command onto the battlefield as to a funeral rite!
stops.quote_source: Officers of the 37th battalion to Bem at Déva, August 1849, recorded by János Czetz in Bem erdélyi hadjárata 1848-49-ben (Pest, 1868), p. 183; own translation from Hungarian
suggested_refs: Czetz, Bem erdélyi hadjárata 1848-49-ben (1868), p. 183
sources: Czetz, Bem erdélyi hadjárata 1848-49-ben (1868), p. 183, verified verbatim

stops.name: Arad, Schlick asks a prisoner his name
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the scene follows Kazinczy's surrender in late August 1849 and Czetz records it without a date
stops.campa: At Arad, General Schlick receives the officers surrendered with Kazinczy and asks each his name and rank. Lieutenant Colonel Inczédy Samu gives an answer that is not a name and not a rank. Schlick, Czetz records, put a hand on his shoulder in respect, and did not lift the court martial's sentence of twelve years in a fortress. This too is a scene Czetz did not witness. He collects it, prints it in 1868, and by printing it makes the sentence the thing that survives instead of the twelve years.
stops.quote: I am that Lieutenant Colonel Inczédy who led the heroic 11th battalion to serve at the hand of the great Bem!
stops.quote_source: Lieutenant Colonel Inczédy Samu to General Schlick at Arad, 1849, recorded by János Czetz in Bem erdélyi hadjárata 1848-49-ben (Pest, 1868), p. XXI; own translation from Hungarian
suggested_refs: Czetz, Bem erdélyi hadjárata 1848-49-ben (1868), p. XXI
sources: Czetz, Bem erdélyi hadjárata 1848-49-ben (1868), p. XXI, verified verbatim

stops.name: Hamburg, the campaign put into print
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unknown, defaulted, and the months of evasion inside Hungary before the escape are undocumented
stops.campa: Czetz evades the Habsburg authorities inside Hungary through the winter after the surrender, escapes to Germany, and surfaces at Hamburg in 1850 with a manuscript. Bem's Feldzug in Siebenbürgen in den Jahren 1848 und 1849 is the campaign written from the inside by the chief of staff who planned it. How he got out, by what road and with whose help, no reachable source says. The book fixes Bem's legend in German print for readers who will never see Transylvania, and it fixes his own name alongside it, which is the only capital he now has.
suggested_refs: Bem's Feldzug in Siebenbürgen in den Jahren 1848 und 1849 (Hamburg, 1850)

stops.name: Paris, among the exiles of 1849
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; residency implied by the general exile itinerary, with no dates or addresses in any source consulted
stops.campa: Paris absorbs part of the honvéd officer corps after 1849, alongside Poles and Italians with the same defeat behind them and the same plan in front of them, and Czetz passes through it in these years. The sources give no date and no address for the interval, only that it falls between the Hamburg book and the Istanbul negotiations. What the exile capitals hold in this decade is a floating community waiting for the next European war to reopen the Hungarian question, and for most of them, Czetz included, it never opens.
suggested_refs: The Hungarian, Polish and Italian emigration in Paris after 1849

stops.name: Istanbul, a legion that is never raised
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed to the Crimean War years; no source consulted gives a precise date
stops.campa: During the Crimean War years Czetz travels to Istanbul, where he and György Klapka negotiate with Ottoman and Western authorities over raising a Hungarian legion against Russia, the power that had crushed their revolution in 1849 by intervening on the Habsburg side. It is the emigration's standard play: turn somebody else's war into leverage for Hungary. Austria stays out of the fighting, the case for the legion dissolves with it, and nothing comes of the negotiations. Czetz moves west again, toward the Alps.
suggested_refs: The Hungarian legion projects of Klapka and Czetz in the Crimean War

stops.name: The Mont Cenis works, measuring mountains for wages
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed to the 1850s; no specific work site within the project is documented and the pin marks the Mont Cenis corridor
stops.campa: Czetz takes engineering work on the Mont Cenis railway in the Alps between France and Italy, the first time the Vienna training is applied to a civil rather than a military problem. Tunnel approach, survey camp or rail bed, the sources do not say; the pin marks a corridor and not an address. He is paid by the season, in a country that is not his, for work that has no rank attached to it. A general with no army earns his living by measuring mountains, and the measuring, not the generalship, is what a country on the far side of the Atlantic will eventually pay him for.
suggested_refs: The Mont Cenis and Fréjus railway works of the 1850s and 1860s

stops.name: Villafranca, the armistice that closes Europe
stops.date_confidence: attested for the armistice; Czetz's physical presence at Villafranca is not confirmed in any source consulted
stops.campa: Czetz has organized a Hungarian legion in Italy for the war against Austria when the armistice signed at Villafranca on the eleventh of July 1859 ends that war before Hungarian independence can be raised in it. He withdraws the legion in disappointment. Whether he stands at Villafranca or hears of it at a distance the sources do not establish. What the date establishes is the closing of the strategy pursued since Istanbul: no European war will be turned into a Hungarian one. The exile who spent a decade angling for a war finds instead a country.
suggested_refs: The Armistice of Villafranca, 11 July 1859

stops.name: Seville, the marriage that decides the continent
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed to about 1859; the sources place the meeting and marriage in Spain before the 1860 emigration but give no date
stops.campa: In Seville Czetz meets General Prudencio Ortiz de Rozas, brother of Juan Manuel de Rosas and himself an exile, and marries his daughter Basilia. English accounts say plainly that the marriage is what convinced him his future lay in Argentina, which places it before the crossing and not after. Hungarian accounts that put the wedding in Buenos Aires in 1860 have the geography backwards. A Transylvanian general and an Argentine dictator's niece marry in Andalusia, and a country neither of them was born in acquires its first military academy out of it.
suggested_refs: The exile household of General Prudencio Ortiz de Rozas in Spain

stops.name: Port of Buenos Aires, the name changed at the gangplank
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: In 1860 Czetz steps off ten years of European exile onto the quay at Buenos Aires and becomes Juan Fernando Czetz. He carries a Hungarian general's rank, an engineer's training from Vienna and a marriage into the Rosas family, and none of it guarantees anything here. Argentine regulation reserves general's rank for the native-born, so the youngest general of the honvéd army will serve his new country as a colonel for forty-four years. The country is still assembling itself out of decades of civil war and has no idea yet what it needs him for.
suggested_refs: The Argentine regulation reserving general's rank for the native-born

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the surveyor's licence revalidated
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: In 1861 Czetz revalidates his land surveyor's licence, converting the Vienna cartographic training into an Argentine civilian credential, and goes out to measure the south of Buenos Aires province. It is unglamorous work after a European general's career: chains and theodolites instead of a staff. The border maps, the frontier line, the town plats and the provincial cadastre all follow from that credential. He is thirty-nine and beginning a second career on foot, in a province he reached the year before and has to measure before he can be paid for it.
suggested_refs: The Argentine surveyor's licence, revalidated 1861

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the borders with Paraguay and Brazil
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed to the 1860s; the sources name an army engineering section and a geographic-military institute without dates or address
stops.campa: Czetz is taken into the engineering section of the Argentine army, reportedly through the influence of Lucio V. Mansilla, and draws the official maps of the republic's borders with Paraguay and Brazil. The institution he works through is named differently in different sources and dated in none of them, so it stands here as a frame and not a building. In 1865 the War of the Triple Alliance makes him a colonel of the Argentine army, and illness keeps him in bed for months of it. A former Transylvanian chief of staff fixes the outer edges of the republic on paper.
suggested_refs: The official Argentine border maps with Paraguay and Brazil, drawn in the 1860s

stops.name: Rojas, the town laid out on the grass
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: In 1866 Czetz plats the town of Rojas on the Buenos Aires pampa, drawing a grid onto ground that has never carried one. It is the surveyor's version of what he had done at Csucsa eighteen years earlier: fixing a line that did not exist until he drew it, and then letting people stand on it. The plat is streets, blocks and a central square laid down before there are houses to fill them. Rojas is built on that plan and stands on it still, which is more than can be said for the line at the pass.
suggested_refs: The 1866 town plan of Rojas, Buenos Aires province

stops.name: Esperanza, the rails toward the colony
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the sources place this railroad planning in the general 1866 period without fixing the dates
stops.campa: Czetz plans railroad and road routes in the Santa Fe region, including the line toward Esperanza, an organized immigrant farming colony rather than a frontier garrison. Two kinds of settlement are being surveyed by the same hand in the same years: the grid town on open pampa and the rail link to a colony of Swiss and German farmers. Between the crossing and the Colegio Militar he spends a decade drawing the infrastructure of the republic: rail lines, roads, town grids, boundary maps, all of it on paper before any of it is on the ground.
suggested_refs: The agricultural colony of Esperanza, Santa Fe, founded 1856

stops.name: General Villegas, the frontier line staked
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: In 1869 Domingo Faustino Sarmiento's government charges Colonel of Engineers Juan Czetz and Colonel Antonio Benavides, head of the southern frontier of Santa Fe, with surveying a new frontier line against the indigenous nations: Fortín Número 8 República, Fuerte Coronel Gainza, Fortín Díaz. Sources disagree about where this happened. English accounts say southern Córdoba; the documented fortines stand in what is now northwestern Buenos Aires province. The disagreement is left standing here. General Rivas rides out to inspect the staked line and tells the surveyor what it is.
stops.quote: My friend, this frontier line of yours will yet cost a few excellent men their lives.
stops.quote_source: General Rivas to Czetz on the new frontier line, quoted in János Czetz, Emlékezéseim (ed. Kedves Gyula, Budaörs, 2001), p. ~124; own translation from Hungarian
suggested_refs: es.wikipedia, 'General Villegas', on the 1869 commission to Czetz and Benavides
sources: Czetz, Emlékezéseim (2001), verified in the digitized MEK PDF

stops.name: The pampa forts, the band at sundown
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the passage is undated in Emlékezéseim and belongs to the 1869 survey expedition
stops.campa: Every evening on the survey expedition the unit's band plays the prayer in the forts at sundown, and Czetz writes that in the solitude of the Pampa it made a great impression on him. He is forty-seven, a Transylvanian who has commanded a province, standing in grass with a theodolite and listening to brass. Ten years later Julio Argentino Roca will launch one of the five columns of the Conquest of the Desert from Trenque Lauquen, along this same borderland. The line Czetz stakes is a survey. What is built on it afterwards is somebody else's campaign.
stops.quote: Every day at sunset, the unit's band played this in the forts. This prayer made me forget the fatigues and privations that both the troops and the officers suffered in this abandoned wilderness.
stops.quote_source: János Czetz, Emlékezéseim (ed. Kedves Gyula, Budaörs, 2001), p. 124, under the section heading 'Esti ima' (Evening prayer); own translation from Hungarian
suggested_refs: Czetz, Emlékezéseim, ed. Kedves Gyula (Budaörs, 2001), digitized at mek.oszk.hu/08500/08509

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the railway directorship declined
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Czetz's own section heading, 'A Colegio Militar megszervezése. 1869'; month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Minister Dalmacio Vélez Sarsfield offers Czetz, on Sarmiento's behalf, the directorship of the Ferrocarril Central Norte. It is the obvious appointment for the man who has been drawing the republic's rail routes for a decade, and he turns it down, because he has already given his word to Minister Gainza that he will build a military academy instead. He records the choice himself, thirty years later, under a heading that gives the year and the task in one line. He takes the school over the railway on the strength of a promise given in conversation.
stops.quote: Here in Buenos Aires, Minister Vélez Sársfield, on Sarmiento's behalf, offered me the directorship of the Ferrocarril Central Norte railway; but I had already promised Minister Gainza that I would undertake the founding of a Colegio Militar.
stops.quote_source: János Czetz, Emlékezéseim (ed. Kedves Gyula, Budaörs, 2001), p. ~125, section 'A Colegio Militar megszervezése. 1869'; own translation from Hungarian
suggested_refs: Czetz, Emlékezéseim, section 'A Colegio Militar megszervezése. 1869'
sources: Czetz, Emlékezéseim (2001), verified in the digitized MEK PDF

stops.name: San Benito de Palermo, the academy established by law
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the eleventh of October 1869 the Colegio Militar de la Nación is established by law under Sarmiento and housed in the San Benito property at Palermo, the caserón that had belonged to Juan Manuel de Rosas and was expropriated by the state after 1852. Accounts that have the building reaching Czetz through his marriage into the Rosas family are inventing a symmetry; no source names a donor. The house of the dictator whose niece he married in Seville becomes, by expropriation rather than by gift, the seedbed of the national military academy.
suggested_refs: The former Rosas caserón at San Benito de Palermo, first seat of the Colegio Militar

stops.name: Palermo, first director of the Colegio Militar
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the twenty-second of June 1870 Colonel Juan Czetz is designated first director of the Colegio Militar de la Nación, and the first courses begin on the nineteenth of July. He holds the post about five years and builds the institution out of nothing, on the European military-academic model he had absorbed as a cadet at Wiener Neustadt and Vienna. The man trained to be an Austrian officer now makes the school that trains Argentine ones. Forty-one years later a cadet named Juan Domingo Perón will enter it, by then moved out to El Palomar.

stops.name: Paraná, the cadastre of Entre Ríos
stops.date_confidence: attested from 1875 onward; month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: From 1875 Czetz heads the topographic department of Entre Ríos at Paraná and produces the cadastral and topographic plans of the entire province. It is the same discipline at a provincial scale: property lines, land titles, administrative boundaries across a territory that has never been systematically measured. He is fifty-three when he starts. The honvéd chief of staff who took Nagyszeben spends his later working years fixing where one Argentine estancia ends and the next begins. The province becomes governable on paper before it is governed on the ground.
suggested_refs: The cadastral and topographic plans of Entre Ríos, from 1875

stops.name: Buenos Aires, thirty-five years and retirement
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Czetz retires in 1895, thirty-five years after stepping off a ship into a country where he had no guaranteed place. Behind him: a surveyor's licence, the border maps, the town of Rojas, a line of forts on the pampa, the first directorship of the national military academy, the cadastre of a province. He also wrote a treatise on permanent and temporary fortification, which no source consulted troubles to date. He is seventy-three and has nine years left, and the thing that occupies them is not the work but the distance from Gidófalva.
suggested_refs: Czetz's treatise on permanent and temporary fortification, undated in the sources

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the letter to Deáky
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed to c. 1900-1903, the premiership of Kálmán Széll; the letter itself is undated in the source
stops.campa: Prime Minister Kálmán Széll raises the old general's Hungarian pension from 1,920 to 4,000 korona and lets it be known he would go to 8,000 a year if Czetz came home. Czetz answers Albert Deáky of the museum of military relics with one sentence about what he already knows will happen. His doctors advise against the voyage and his daughter Krisztina has a serious lung disease. The letter survives on a Hungarian scout troop's web page and from there into the encyclopedias, which is a thin chain for the most quoted thing he ever wrote.
stops.quote: I am already an old man, so long removed from my homeland, and yet, because of homesickness, my heart still aches with the knowledge that I must find my rest in foreign soil.
stops.quote_source: János Czetz, letter to Albert Deáky, quoted on hu.wikipedia, 'Czetz János', footnoted to Jakab Erzsébet, rmcssz.ro
suggested_refs: The pension correspondence with the Széll government, c. 1900-1903

stops.name: Buenos Aires, death at eighty-two
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the sixth of September 1904 Juan Fernando Czetz dies in Buenos Aires at eighty-two: twenty-seven years a Habsburg cadet, honvéd general and stateless exile, forty-four years an Argentine officer and surveyor. Eleven years later, in this same city, Emin Arslan's weekly La Nota will carry to Argentine readers among the first word of the Armenian deportations, in the language of a country that had taken them both in. No flag covers the whole of Czetz's life, and the Armenian half of it was never proved.
suggested_refs: The Buenos Aires Armenian community, whose institutions postdate Czetz by a generation

stops.name: Recoleta, the vault of the Ortiz de Rozas
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the day of interment is not given in the sources and is defaulted within the month of death
stops.campa: He is laid in the Cementerio de la Recoleta among the mausoleums of the Argentine elite, in the family vault of the Ortiz de Rozas and not in a tomb of his own. The marriage made in Seville forty-five years earlier is what puts him there. A Székely from Háromszék, catalogued in Budapest as of Armenian origin, rests in the necropolis of the founding families of Buenos Aires, in a stranger's vault, under a name he adopted at forty. He will not stay sixty-five years.
suggested_refs: The Ortiz de Rozas family vault, Cementerio de la Recoleta

stops.name: El Palomar, the chapel on the centenary
stops.date_confidence: year attested for the transfer, made during the academy's centennial; month and day not given, defaulted
stops.campa: In 1969, the hundredth year of the school created by law in October 1869, his remains are moved from Recoleta to the chapel of the Colegio Militar de la Nación, by then relocated to El Palomar. The first Spanish plaque called him an Argentine colonel and the academy's first director and said nothing about Hungary. After requests from Argentina's Hungarian community a second inscription was added: a Hungarian general and Transylvanian commander sleeps his eternal sleep here. No source gives the year of the second plaque. Two countries wrote on the same stone, one of them late.
suggested_refs: The chapel of the Colegio Militar de la Nación at El Palomar, holding Czetz's remains since 1969

stops.name: Gyergyószentmiklós, the relief in the Armenian courtyard
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the relief is attested but its date of installation is not given in any source consulted
stops.campa: A relief of Czetz is set in the courtyard of the Armenian Catholic church at Gyergyószentmiklós, one of the two Armenian foundation towns of Transylvania, alongside Szamosújvár where the family name is said to have been recorded in 1715. The claim the archive never confirmed is carved here as if it were settled. No document has turned up in the meantime and none is waited for. What stands instead is a face on a wall, put there by the community that claims him, in the courtyard of its own church.
suggested_refs: The Armenian Catholic church of Gyergyószentmiklós (Gheorgheni), Romania

stops.name: Óbuda, a street in the third district
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the street name is attested but the date of naming is not given in any source consulted and the pin is the district, not the street
stops.campa: Czetz János utca runs in the third district of Budapest, in Óbuda, with memorial plaques at its entrance. He never lived in Budapest. He passed through Pest at twenty-two to publish a manual, and through it again at twenty-six on his way out of the imperial army, and after 1850 he never saw the city or the country again. The street is the address Hungary gave a man who died asking for one and was told, in the end, that the pension was the best it could do.
suggested_refs: Czetz János utca, Budapest District III, with memorial plaques at its entrance

stops.name: Gidófalva, the plaque on the town hall wall
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the plaque is attested but no source consulted dates its installation
stops.campa: On the wall of the village hall at Gidófalva there is a memorial tablet, not a monument. It is the smallest of the markers and it stands on the only ground in the story that was ever unambiguously his. In 1916 Fritz Lang was deployed to the Transylvanian front, ninety-four years after the birth in this village and sixty-seven after the pass at Csucsa, and the same mountains were fought over again by an empire that no longer had this family in its officer corps. The house is gone. The tablet gives the dates.
suggested_refs: The memorial tablet on the village hall at Gidófalva (Ghidfalău), Covasna, Romania

stops.name: Békásmegyer, the horse he is finally given
stops.date_confidence: attested for the unveiling; the pin is Lékai Bíboros tér in Békásmegyer, located approximately
stops.campa: On the fourth of October 2019 an equestrian statue of Czetz is unveiled at Lékai Bíboros tér in Békásmegyer, in the same Budapest district as his street. In front of the Argentine military academy he stands on his own feet: the bronze there is life-size and standing, and a bust is kept inside the building. Hungary gives him the horse. The riding accident of the twenty-ninth of May 1849 ended his war, and a hundred and seventy years later the country he could not return to puts him back on a horse in a square he never saw.
suggested_refs: The equestrian statue of Czetz at Lékai Bíboros tér, Békásmegyer, unveiled 4 October 2019
